1.      Introduction
    A monotone Boolean circuit is a circuit that only uses the monotone gates ∧, ∨; negations
are not allowed. One of the beautiful success stories of complexity theory has been the
achievement of exponential monotone circuit lower bounds. In this paper, we prove new
monotone circuit lower bounds for detecting matchings, and simplify the proofs of some
other monotone circuit lower bounds for natural functions.
    In a foundational paper, Razborov [20] proved that computing matching and detecting
cliques both require monotone circuits of size nΩ(log n) . Alon and Boppana [1] later improved

concept of sunflowers, namely a collection of sets whose pairwise intersections are identical.
Erdős and Rado [10] showed that every large collection of small sets must contain a large
sunflower, and Razborov used this sunflower lemma to approximate the gates of a given
monotone circuit with simpler functions, yielding circuit lower bounds. Since then, similar
monotone circuit lower bounds were also proved by appealing to the switching lemma or
other methods which avoided the use of sunflowers altogether [13, 5, 14]. Another direction
leveraged the connection to communication complexity to prove optimal lower bounds of
Ω(n) on the depth of the monotone circuits computing clique or matching [19, 18].

1.1.     Robust sunflowers and spreadness
   A significant advance in the study of these monotone circuit lower bounds was made
by Rossman [21] when he introduced the notion of robust sunflowers. Loosely speaking, a
robust sunflower is a DNF, namely a formula in disjunctive normal form, with the property

                                                        1


                                                                                                ISSN 1433-8092
that the DNF can be approximated by a single term. Rossman’s work revealed that robust
sunflowers could be used to prove new monotone circuit lower bounds. For example, he gave
exponential monotone circuit lower bounds for the task of distinguishing graphs with cliques
of size k from Erdős-Renyi random graphs that do not have such cliques.
    In a breakthrough, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [2] established an essentially optimal
robust sunflower lemma. The proof crucially used the concept of a spread set, first considered
by Talagrand [22]. We say that a random set X is r-spread if for all sets S,

                                       p(S ⊆ X) ≤ r−|S| .

Let X to denote the support of X. The key contribution of [2] is a nice encoding argument
to show that a random set must contain some element of a spread family X with high
probability. Subsequent work by myself [16], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park [11],
and Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke [4] cleaned up the bounds to obtain the following version
(see [17] for the easiest proof):

Lemma 1 (Spread Set Lemma). There is a universal constant α > 0 such that the following
holds. Let ε ≤ 1/2, r = α log(t/ε)/γ and X be a random r-spread set of size at most t. Then
if Y is a random set including each element independently with probability γ,

                                  p(∃x ∈ X , x ⊆ Y ) > 1 − ε.

    If a monotone DNF has terms that correspond to X , then the conclusion of Lemma 1
is that the DNF can be approximated by the function 1 from the perspective of a random
input Y . Lemma 1 is tight [2]. Let [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n}, let f : [t] → [⌈log(t/ε)/γ⌉] be a
uniformly random function, and let X = {(i, f (i))} be its graph. Then X is r-spread with
r = ⌈log(t/ε)/γ⌉, but if Y includes each element with probability γ, the probability that Y
is disjoint from [i] × [⌈log(t/ε)/γ⌉] is

                            (1 − γ)⌈log(t/ε)/γ⌉ ≈ eγ⌈log(t/ε)/γ⌉ ≈ ε/t,

so Y does not contain the graph of any f with probability ≈ ε.

1.2.    Our results
   In this paper, we give new monotone circuit lower bounds for detecting matchings.

Theorem 3. For q < k ≤ n/2, any monotone circuit that can distinguish n-vertex bipartite
graphs with
          √ matchings of size k from graphs that do not have matchings of size q must have
exp(Ω(q/( k log n)) gates.

   Setting k = n/2, q = n/4 yields:

Corollary 4. Any monotone circuit that can distinguish n-vertex bipartite graphs with a
perfect √
        matching from graphs that do not have matchings of size n/4 must have
exp(Ω( n/ log n)) gates.

     Corollary 4 improves on the results of [7] in two ways: the exponent is larger, and
the lower bound applies for distinguishing perfect matchings from graphs with no small
matchings, rather than distinguishing perfect matchings from graphs with matchings of size
n − 2. Theorem 3 gives exponential lower bounds even for circuits that distinguish graphs
with matchings of size n1/5 from graphs that do not have matchings of size n1/9 .
     Following the usual pattern, these new results are a consequence of a new spread matching
lemma with essentially optimal parameters. We say that a random matching X is r-spread
if for every matching m,
                                       p(m ⊆ X) ≤ r−|m| .
Let G(W ) denote the graph that contains exactly those edges that are incident to W .

Lemma 5 (Spread Matching Lemma). There is a universal constant α > 0 such that the
following holds. Let ε < 1/2, t > 1, r = α · (log t)2 · (t + log2 (1/ε))/γ 2 , and X be a random
r-spread matching on the set of vertices [n], with |X| ≤ t. Then if W ⊆ [n] is a uniformly
random set with |W | = γn,

                               p(∃x ∈ X , x ⊆ G(W )) > 1 − ε.

    Corollary 7 looks closer to a statement proved in [7]. To prove it, let X ∈ X be uniform,
and pick the largest matching m violating r-spreadness. Then X \ m | X ∈ M is guaranteed
to be r-spread by the choice of m, so we can apply Lemma 5 to derive the conclusion. The
main improvement of Lemma 5 and Corollary 7 over the corresponding statement of [7] is
the dependence of r on t and ε. Our dependence is of the type t + log2 (1/ε), while theirs is
t log2 (1/ε). Our results apply using the graph G(W ), which contains a matching of size at
most γn, while their result required the use of graphs that contain matchings of size n − 2.
    The proof of Lemma 5 is not as easy as the old one. It uses a new encoding argument
tailored for matchings, and the argument is, unfortunately, quite subtle. We prove the
lemma in Section 2, where we also give several examples that verify the (near) optimality of
its parameters. One of the examples given there shows that r ≥ Ω(log2 (1/ε)) is necessary
to obtain error ε.

2.     Spread matching lemma
   In this section, we prove Lemma 1. Here are some examples that show why Lemma 5
has must have the form that it does:

  1. Let A and B be disjoint sets, each of size log(1/ε)/2, and X be a single random edge
     from A to B. Let γ = 1/2. Then X is r-spread with r = log(1/ε)2 /4, yet with
     probability ≈ ε, G(W ) does not include any edge in the support of X. This shows
     that r ≥ Ω(log2 (1/ε)) is required.

  2. Let A and B be disjoint sets of size t, and X be a uniformly random perfect matching
     from A to B. Then X is r-spread with r = t/2. If γ = 1/3, with probability > 1/2,
     W contains less than t of the vertices of A ∪ B, so the probability that G(W ) contains
     one of the matchings is at most 1/2. This shows that (t/2)-spreadness is necessary,
     even to achieve error 1/2.

  3. Let X be a uniformly random matching of size t = λn/2 from [n/2] to [n] \ [n/2].
     Then X is Θ(n/λ)-spread. However, if γ < λ/2, we see that G(W ) cannot contain any
     matching of size t. This shows that r ≪ t/γ 2 is insufficient.

  4. Let X be a uniformly random edge from the star graph, namely the set of edges
     {{1, j} : j > 1}. We see that X is (n − 1)-spread, yet W contains an edge of X only if
     it contains 1, and this happens with probability at most γ. This example shows why
     edges not contained in W need to be included in G(W ).
